text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Interest rates have fallen to unprecedented lows, helping home owners and the Swedish state. Rents have, however, continued to increase.

- The chief executive of Swedish bank Nordbanken said he still thinks a merger between the bank and rival S-E-Banken would be a good idea. Merger talks between the bank failed at the beginning of February.

- Carl Bildt, the international mediator in Bosnia and the leader of the Swedish conservatives, the Moderate Party, is in hospital in Stockholm after catching a suspected viral infection in Sarajevo. Bildt has cancelled all meetings until Wednesday.
- About 25 percent of Stockholm residents needed state benefits sometime last year in order to make ends meet.

- Negotiationas between Swedish construction and real estate companies Siab and NCC only took three days and if more mergers take place they would be with foreign partners, according to NCC's chairman Bernt Magnusson.

- There is a fight about which standard will prevail in Nordic digital television as competitors Multichoice and Modern Times Group (MTG), controlled by Swedish holding company Kinnevik, are competing with different standards.

- Top managers in Sweden's biggest companies say they have powerful members of the business community behind a vote of no confidence about the country's business policies which was published over the weekend in Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter.

- The the financial arm of the Swedish Wallenburg family's business empire, Swedish investment group Investor AB, is now larger than the country's Fourth AP pension fund as an owner on the Stockholm Stock Exchange.

- The wife of Bosnia mediator Carl Bildt, who is in a Stockholm hospital for a suspected viral infection, says he is feeling fine and his situation is stable but he must remain in the hospital for observation.

- Over the next month a record 32.6 billion crowns will be paid out in dividends in Sweden to investors in bonds and stocks. Much of the money is expected to find its way back to the Stockholm Stock Exchange.

- Mineral unit Boliden, whose parent company Trelleborg says it will spin off and list, will receive new life when it is listed on the Toronto stock exchange. Previously it had to turn down many projects but now it will be open to a whole new world of risk capital.

- Luxury glass and porcelain retail chain Duka will be sold by its owner Goran Nord to Norwegian glass and porcelain maker Atle Brynestad. The chain is made up of 29 stores and has an annual turnover of 725 million crowns.
